extracted.intended_audience: researchers in neuroscience and philosophy interested in laughter/humor and neuroimaging
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and interpreting empirical investigations of laughter and humor that integrate philosophical theorizing, phenomenology, and human functional neuroimaging (particularly fNIRS and dynamical-systems approaches).

rubrics_metrics.name: Antilocalizationist / dynamical-systems approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer investigating laughter using antilocalizationist, whole-brain and dynamical-systems methods rather than focusing solely on localization of functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metrics derived from dynamical systems (e.g., metastability) to characterize global brain dynamics and the balance between integration and segregation. Integrate these approaches with classic localizationist findings rather than discarding them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat laughter as embodied and socially embedded
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigations should recognize laughter as an eminently embodied, interactive, and socially situated phenomenon rather than an isolated individual response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design studies and interpretations that account for embodiment, social reciprocity, and interpersonal dynamics (e.g., study dyads, conversational contexts). Avoid reducing laughter to purely intrapersonal signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fNIRS for production and ecologically valid settings
rubrics_metrics.description: Because fMRI is highly sensitive to motion, use functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to probe brain function during laughter production in more naturalistic and freely moving participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage fNIRS for its lower susceptibility to motion artefacts and ease of adaptation to hyperscanning paradigms; note its limitation to sparsely sampled cortical areas and plan complementary methods if subcortical data are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rest–task–rest experimental paradigm
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ a rest–task–rest design to compare global brain dynamics before, during, and after laughter (baseline → spontaneous laughter → post-laughter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This paradigm allows characterizing the full cycle of pleasure and testing changes in metrics such as metastability across the three phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include control conditions to dissociate movement and stimulus effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Include controls such as voluntary (posed) laughter and watching non-humorous videos to determine whether observed differences are due to movement, voluntary production, or stimulus features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare involuntary/spontaneous laughter to voluntary laughter and nonhumorous stimuli to isolate effects attributable to humor and involuntariness versus motion or other confounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful first-person phenomenological reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect detailed first-person descriptions or interviews during/after data acquisition to establish whether laughter was experienced as humorous (mirth) and to capture phenomenology of concurrent affective states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask participants whether they felt something was funny when they laughed and why; integrate these reports with neuroimaging to link subjective experience to neural dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure and interpret metastability as index of global cognitive state
rubrics_metrics.description: Use metastability (balance between integration and segregation in large-scale networks) as a key metric to index global cognitive states and cognitive flexibility related to laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret higher metastability as associated with increased cognitive flexibility and an 'offline' mode (DMN activation, decoupling from immediate affordances); interpret lower metastability as an 'online' focused attentional mode. Use these interpretations to form testable hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses linking laughter to metastability and cognitive flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulate and test explicit hypotheses: (a) involuntary laughter will increase metastability relative to resting-state; (b) after laughing, metastability should increase further (consistent with Relief Theory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are pragmatically testable predictions using fNIRS and dynamical-systems analyses; state them explicitly in registered designs and pre-registrations where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine naturalistic stimuli and resting-state paradigms
rubrics_metrics.description: Use naturalistic stimuli (e.g., humorous videos, movies) and resting-state paradigms rather than tightly constrained cognitive tasks to capture flexible, ecologically valid brain dynamics associated with laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naturalistic and less constrained settings can increase metastability and reveal global brain modes relevant to humor and spontaneous laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate voluntary vs involuntary laughter empirically
rubrics_metrics.description: Discriminate voluntary (non-Duchenne) and involuntary (Duchenne) laughter using acoustic, expression, and physiological markers because they differ in authenticity, tonal variability, intensity, and associated affect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use established acoustic/perceptual criteria (e.g., greater tonal variability and perceived authenticity for involuntary laughter) and include these distinctions in analysis and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for movement artefacts and methodological limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly account for motion artefacts (a major limitation for fMRI laughter production studies) and methodological sampling limits (e.g., fNIRS restricted to cortical regions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer modalities less susceptible to motion for production studies; when using fMRI, restrict to perception tasks or use modeling/controls to mitigate motion confounds. Plan complementary approaches (e.g., computational modeling, simultaneous stimulation) to probe subcortical dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use hyperscanning and between-brain / social-neuroscience metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: To capture the central social nature of laughter, use fNIRS hyperscanning and analyze emerging between-brain properties and social coupling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyperscanning enables study of dyadic interactions and affiliation/contagion dynamics; integrate social metrics and information-theoretic measures where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate philosophical theories into empirical hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Use established philosophical/theoretical frameworks of humor (Incongruity, Relief, Superiority, Bergson's account, Benign Violation, SSTH) to motivate and interpret empirical predictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate philosophical claims into testable predictions about brain dynamics (e.g., incongruity → increased flexibility/metastability; relief → post-laughter increases in metastability) and be explicit about which theory each prediction tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine neuroimaging with computational modeling and stimulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Where subcortical mechanisms or mechanistic integration between networks are implicated, combine fNIRS/fMRI with computational whole-brain models and/or simultaneous stimulation to test causal hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider fMRI and computational modeling to indirectly test subcortical contributions; where feasible, use simultaneous stimulation and imaging to probe causal roles of candidate nodes (e.g., nucleus accumbens, anterior cingulate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider individual differences and developmental/age effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for age-related and individual variability (e.g., younger participants showing greater reward-circuit involvement; older participants showing stronger DMN activation) when designing studies and interpreting results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include sufficient sampling across ages or analyze age as a moderator; consider baseline receptor availability and other individual predictors that may influence laughter frequency and neural responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use registered reports and open, negative-result reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt registered reports and commit to publishing negative results to prevent others from pursuing dead ends and to clarify which theoretical predictions are supported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-register hypotheses and experimental designs (the authors reference a registered report) and ensure transparent reporting of null/negative outcomes.
